name: Kalmykia
summary_text: Kalmykia, an autonomous republic of the Russian Federation, is assessed under the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (version 2.0, June 2025). That note records that consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. The note contains no Kalmykia-specific information; the national framework sets the standard for what a transgender visitor to the republic should expect.  Legal gender recognition is prohibited outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. A 2024 law additionally bars adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes, which since their December 2022 expansion reach material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships, making minors interested in gender transition, or giving minors a "desire to change their sex"; the provisions cover speech that justifies gender transition. Penalties reach fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, and repeated offences risk criminal prosecution. The UK Home Office note records that at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024. Human Rights Watch counted 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of an "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years in prison, for participation in that movement or display of its symbols. The same organisation documented 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media. Within 48 hours of the designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations were outlawed as extremist.  Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented: a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour.  Entry and onward protection carry explicit warnings. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles transgender Russians caught between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians; for many, emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly.

name: Karachay-Cherkessia
summary_text: Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition has been prohibited outright since President Vladimir Putin signed the law in 2023. The statute bans gender reassignment surgery, forbids any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and strips the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria. A visitor presenting documents whose marker does not match their presentation has no lawful route to resolve the discrepancy inside the country.  Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law addressed material concerning minors and was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups, reaching content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, gives minors a "desence to change their sex", or justifies gender transition. Enforcement has accelerated: more than 180 cases were brought under the provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines; cases have risen eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.  Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, displaying the rainbow flag or its colours has drawn charges. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, with at least two further venues raided the same night. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions as of 30 June 2025, drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes, and between March and May 2026 nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.  The North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, is treated as worse than the national baseline. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory finding on Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with systematic regional campaigns documented across 2017 to 2024. The same note records that the 2023 extremist designation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment, rising to 6 to 10 years for organising. David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, an on-the-ground defender now in exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he reports year-on-year deterioration across the North Caucasus republics, which include Karachay-Cherkessia.  Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. In summer 2021 a transgender woman was lured by relatives to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.  Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. The 2024 law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions bears on foreign visitors with residence status.  Entry and onward-protection context: the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers, and the UK Home Office note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.
